ety.text: From Middle English eddy, from Old English edēa, from ed- (“turning, back, reverse”) + ēa (“water”), equivalent to ed- + ea. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁é, and, consequently, cognate with Latin et. Related also to Danish ide (“eddy”), Swedish eda (“eddy”), Norwegian ida, ia, ea (“eddy”), Icelandic iða (“eddy”).

senses.d: A current of air or water running back, or in an opposite direction to the main current.

ex: And smiling eddies dimpled on the main.
Wheel through the air, in circling eddies play.

senses.d: To form an eddy; to move in, or as if in, an eddy; to move in a circle.
ex: He waded out, the stream eddying around his legs.
It’s a uniquely American news story, one that eddies until it surges, and then, after it has mostly receded from view, surges again.
These eddies are made with both fruits and veggies, and weed of course, with cozy flavor profiles like honey lemon and apple pie.

grp.label: air or water running in an opposite direction to the main current
